subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The Rise of the SUV
description: A fast breakdown of The Rise of the SUV for builders.

hook.text: SUVs were built for off-road work. Somehow they became America's favorite family car.

buildup.text: In the 1990s, automakers realized SUVs had a loophole—lower fuel economy rules than regular cars.

discovery.text: They also had enormous profit margins. A Ford Explorer made five times more profit than a sedan.

twist.text: Buyers loved the size, the height, and the feeling of safety—even though SUVs rolled over more easily.

climax.text: By 2020, trucks and SUVs made up 75% of US vehicle sales. The sedan nearly went extinct.

quiz.question: Why did automakers love selling SUVs?

details.summary: SUVs evolved from rugged military Jeeps and work trucks into luxurious family vehicles, exploiting a regulatory loophole that exempted them from the stricter fuel economy rules applied to cars.
details.whyItMatters: The SUV boom reshaped the auto industry and American fuel consumption. Their popularity and profit margins saved Detroit's Big Three financially while increasing overall emissions.
takeaways: SUVs were classified as light trucks with looser fuel economy rules
Profit margins on SUVs were far higher than on sedans
The Ford Explorer launched the mainstream SUV era in 1990

faq.question: Why are SUVs so profitable for automakers?
faq.answer: SUVs use truck platforms that are cheaper to build, command higher sticker prices due to perceived ruggedness, and offer lucrative option packages. Margins can be five to ten times those of a compact sedan.

faq.question: Did SUVs increase overall fuel consumption in America?
faq.answer: Yes. Despite individual efficiency improvements, the shift from sedans to heavier SUVs offset gains from engine technology. The average weight and fuel consumption of new vehicles rose through the 2000s.
